questions.stem: What is the oxidation state of iron in K$_4$[Fe(CN)$_6$]?
questions.explanation: Four K$^+$ ions balance the charge of the complex ion, so the complex ion is [Fe(CN)$_6$]$^{4-}$. Each cyanide carries a charge of -1, so six of them give -6. Hence $x - 6 = -4$ and the oxidation state of iron is +2.

optionRationale.1: +3 is the oxidation state of iron in K$_3$[Fe(CN)$_6$].
optionRationale.3: No standard hexacyanidoferrate complex has iron in +4.
optionRationale.4: Zero would apply for a neutral complex such as Fe(CO)$_5$.

questions.objective: Find the oxidation state of the central metal ion

questions.stem: The denticity of the ligand ethylenediaminetetraacetate (EDTA$^{4-}$) is
questions.explanation: EDTA$^{4-}$ binds through two nitrogen atoms and four carboxylate oxygen atoms, so it can occupy six coordination sites on the metal ion. It is therefore a hexadentate ligand and forms very stable chelates.

optionRationale.2: Four counts only the carboxylate oxygens and ignores the two nitrogen donors.
optionRationale.4: EDTA has six donor atoms, not three.

questions.stem: The IUPAC name of K$_3$[Fe(CN)$_6$] is
questions.explanation: In the anionic complex the ligands are named first in alphabetical order, followed by the metal with the ending -ate. The ligand is cyanido (six of them, hexa), and iron becomes ferrate. The oxidation state is +3 since three K$^+$ balance [Fe(CN)$_6$]$^{3-}$.

optionRationale.1: The oxidation state (II) belongs to K$_4$[Fe(CN)$_6$].
optionRationale.2: The cations are not given numerical prefixes, and the central metal is named as ferrate, not iron.
optionRationale.3: The complex anion is named as one unit with the metal ending in -ate, not as a separate cyanide.

questions.objective: Apply IUPAC naming to an anionic complex

questions.stem: The spin-only magnetic moment of [CoF$_6$]$^{3-}$ (F$^-$ is a weak field ligand; Co atomic number 27) is closest to
questions.explanation: Co$^{3+}$ is 3d$^6$. With the weak field ligand F$^-$ the splitting is small, so electrons stay unpaired in the high-spin arrangement t$_{2g}^4$ e$_g^2$, giving four unpaired electrons. The moment is $\sqrt{4 \times 6} = 4.90$ BM.

optionRationale.2: Zero would be the value for the low-spin diamagnetic complex [Co(NH$_3$)$_6$]$^{3+}$.
optionRationale.3: This is the value for two unpaired electrons.
optionRationale.4: This is the value for three unpaired electrons.

questions.objective: Calculate the magnetic moment of a high-spin complex

questions.stem: Which of the following is a homoleptic complex?
questions.explanation: A homoleptic complex has only one kind of ligand bonded to the metal. [Co(NH$_3$)$_6$]$^{3+}$ has only ammonia, so it is homoleptic. The others carry two different kinds of ligands, so they are heteroleptic.

optionRationale.1: It has both NH$_3$ and Cl$^-$ ligands, so it is heteroleptic.
optionRationale.3: It has NH$_3$ and Cl$^-$ ligands in the same complex, so it is heteroleptic even though it is neutral.
optionRationale.4: It has both en and Cl$^-$ ligands, so it is heteroleptic.

questions.stem: In metal carbonyls the metal-carbon bond has both sigma and pi character. The pi bond is formed by
options: donation of the lone pair of CO into a vacant metal orbital
overlap of a filled $\pi$ orbital of CO with an s orbital of the metal
donation of electrons from a filled metal d orbital into a vacant antibonding $\pi^*$ orbital of CO
ionic attraction between the metal ion and the carbon atom of CO
questions.explanation: The sigma bond arises when the lone pair on carbon is donated into a vacant metal orbital. The metal then donates electron density from a filled d orbital back into the vacant antibonding $\pi^*$ orbital of CO. This synergic back donation strengthens the M-C bond.

optionRationale.1: This describes the sigma bond, not the pi bond.
optionRationale.2: An s orbital cannot overlap in a pi fashion with a filled pi orbital.
optionRationale.4: The M-C bond in carbonyls is covalent, with zero or low oxidation state metal.

questions.objective: Explain synergic bonding in metal carbonyls

questions.stem: Which of the following octahedral complexes is optically active?
questions.explanation: An optically active complex has a non-superimposable mirror image. The cis isomer of [CoCl$_2$(en)$_2$]$^+$ lacks a plane of symmetry and exists as a pair of enantiomers. The trans isomer, [Co(NH$_3$)$_6$]$^{3+}$ and fac-[Co(NH$_3$)$_3$Cl$_3$] each have a plane of symmetry and are optically inactive.

optionRationale.1: The trans isomer has a plane of symmetry and is achiral.
optionRationale.2: The hexaammine complex is perfectly symmetrical.
optionRationale.3: The facial isomer has a mirror plane through the three ligands of each kind.

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): The square planar complex [PtCl$_2$(NH$_3$)$_2$] shows optical isomerism.
Reason (R): The square planar complex has a plane of symmetry, the plane of the molecule.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: [PtCl$_2$(NH$_3$)$_2$] shows geometrical (cis and trans) isomerism, not optical isomerism. The molecular plane itself acts as a mirror plane, so the complex and its mirror image are superimposable. The reason is therefore true while the assertion is false.

optionRationale.1: The assertion is false, so (R) cannot explain it.
optionRationale.2: The assertion is false, so this option is wrong.
optionRationale.3: The reason is true: the plane of the square is a plane of symmetry.

questions.objective: Recognise isomerism in square planar complexes

questions.stem: Match the complex in List-I with the number of unpaired electrons in List-II.
questions.explanation: Fe$^{2+}$ is d$^6$. With strong field CN$^-$ it is low spin with no unpaired electrons (A-I), and with weak field water it is high spin with four unpaired electrons (B-III). Mn$^{2+}$ is d$^5$ with five unpaired electrons in water (C-IV). Cr$^{3+}$ is d$^3$ with three unpaired electrons (D-II).

optionRationale.2: This code interchanges the matches of A and B; the correct pairs are A-I and B-III.
optionRationale.3: This code interchanges the matches of C and D; the correct pairs are C-IV and D-II.
optionRationale.4: This code interchanges the matches of A and C; the correct pairs are A-I and C-IV.

questions.objective: Predict unpaired electrons in octahedral complexes

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about coordination compounds.
A. A ligand donates at least one lone pair of electrons to the central metal and acts as a Lewis base.
B. EDTA$^{4-}$ is a hexadentate ligand.
C. The oxidation number of cobalt in [Co(NH$_3$)$_6$]$^{3+}$ is +3.
D. The chloride ion is a bidentate ligand.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Ligands are Lewis bases that donate lone pairs, EDTA has six donor atoms, and in [Co(NH$_3$)$_6$]$^{3+}$ the neutral ammonia ligands leave cobalt at +3. The chloride ion has one donor atom, so it is monodentate and D is wrong.

optionRationale.1: D is wrong because chloride is monodentate, and C is also correct.
optionRationale.3: D is wrong because chloride is monodentate, and A is also correct.
optionRationale.4: It includes the wrong statement D and omits the correct statements B and C.

questions.objective: Recall basic definitions in coordination chemistry
